title: The Phulkian states
hook: Patiala, Nabha and Jind, often counted apart from the twelve

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shaheedan misl, named for shaheed, those who gave their lives. Your line was the martyrs' band. Whose name did you say out loud? Today, a family of chiefs who stood a little to one side. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

A hungry boy is brought before Guru Har Rai. Sikh tradition tells it simply: an uncle brings two small brothers to the Guru, and one of them pats his own empty stomach. The Guru looks at the child and blesses him: his house will grow, and it will feed many. The boy's name was Phul. Generations later, the families who traced their line to him ruled three states south of the Sutlej: Patiala, Nabha and Jind. Today: the Phulkian states.
screen: `A HUNGRY BOY BEFORE GURU HAR RAI.` → `A BLESSING ON HIS HOUSE.` → `PATIALA, NABHA AND JIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle the Phulkian states set for anyone who counts the misls. Some lists of the twelve misls include them. Others set them apart. Both habits have reasons. The first reason for setting them apart is the river. The Phulkian chiefs held the Malwa country, south of the Sutlej, and that was their whole world. Different neighbors, different dangers, different deals. The second reason is how they ruled. A misl, as this block has described it, was a band of equals around a chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa. The Phulkian houses grew more like ruling families: the leadership passing down a line, the chief becoming a raja. Patiala's founder, Ala Singh, is remembered for building a state, and for making terms with the powers around him at times when other bands were fighting them. Sikh histories judge those terms in more than one way. Some call them shrewd survival. Some call them a step away from the Dal Khalsa. So why are they in this block at all? Because the story starts with the Guru's blessing. The Phulkian families traced their rise to that hungry boy and that hand on his head, and they built and supported gurdwaras across their lands. They stood apart in politics, and they stayed inside the same faith, the same scripture, the same Guru's house. A family can live in a different town and still sit at the same table on the big days. Apart, yet related.
screen: `SOME LISTS COUNT THEM, SOME DON'T.` · `SOUTH OF THE SUTLEJ, IN MALWA.` · `RULING FAMILIES, NOT BANDS OF EQUALS.` · `ONE GURU'S HOUSE STILL.` · then, large: `APART, YET RELATED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to notice who stands apart. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a group you belong to: a family, a team, a congregation, a group chat. Now find the person who stands a little to the side of it. The cousin who moved away. The coworker who eats lunch alone. The one who does things differently. Don't fix anything. Just hold them in mind, and notice what still connects them to the rest. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Phul, the boy Guru Har Rai blessed, whose line the Phulkian states, Patiala, Nabha and Jind, traced their rule to. Counted with the misls by some, set apart by others. Today's word.
Your line: apart, yet related. Today, reach out to one person who sits at the edge of a group you're in. A message is enough. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

screen: `DAY 899 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWICE A YEAR AT AMRITSAR.`

howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the story of Phul and Guru Har Rai's blessing, and gurdwaras in the former Phulkian lands, such as those in Patiala, are part of Sikh life in the Malwa region today.

fork.setup: you're the uncle who has brought two small boys before Guru Har Rai. one of them pats his empty stomach. what does the Guru do?
options: sends him away to be fed elsewhere.
blesses him, and his house after him.
tells him to come back when he's older.
fork.reveal: tradition says the Guru blessed the boy, Phul, and his house. the families of Patiala, Nabha and Jind traced their rise to that blessing.

trapdoor: what you thought: three more misls on the list.
what it means: three states south of the Sutlej, ruled by families tracing their line to Phul, sometimes counted with the misls and sometimes apart.
what a scholar hears: ruling houses rather than bands of equals, whose dealings with outside powers Sikh histories judge in more than one way.

sources.ref: Phul and Guru Har Rai's blessing; the Phulkian houses, Sikh tradition
sources.work: Rattan Singh Bhangu, Panth Prakash (Sikh tradition)

notes: The Phul story: tellings differ on who brought the boys (Phul and his brother Sandali) and the exact words of the blessing; framed as 'tradition tells it' with variants. Confirm.
The meaning of the name Phul (flower) was cut under the claims rule.
The index says the Phulkian states are 'often counted apart from the twelve'; many standard lists include Phulkian as one of the twelve misls. The script says both habits exist. Confirm.

Ala Singh 'making terms with the powers around him' (including Ahmad Shah Abdali) and Sikh histories judging this 'in more than one way': this is sensitive; a Keeper should confirm the framing is fair to Patiala and to its critics.
'Built and supported gurdwaras across their lands': general; confirm.

Editor: removed the claim that all the other misls held land north of the Sutlej (day 898's Shaheedan were centered at Damdama Sahib, in Malwa); myth item changed to match; softened Ala Singh's terms to 'at times when other bands were fighting them'.

Audit: hook's 'a mother, or an uncle in some tellings' cut to 'an uncle' (the usual tellings name the boys' uncle, Kala; the mother variant could not be supported). Fork no longer casts the listener as Guru Har Rai, since many Sikhs avoid depicting or role-playing the Gurus; the listener is now the uncle. Keeper: confirm.
